common_name: Nicky Garden Phlox (Deep Magenta Mildew-Resistant Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing at least 18 inches apart for air circulation to reduce powdery mildew.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade with good air circulation. Nicky is a longtime garden phlox standard, valued for its vivid magenta-purple flower clusters and notably better resistance to the powdery mildew that disfigures many older garden phlox cultivars by midsummer. It blooms over a long season from midsummer into fall on sturdy, upright stems that generally hold up without staking, drawing butterflies and hummingbirds throughout. Divide congested clumps every 3–4 years in early spring to maintain vigor and airflow, and deadhead spent flower heads to prolong bloom and reduce self-seeding, since seedling phlox often reverts to a washed-out magenta-pink.
sources: Mt. Cuba Center — Phlox Trial Garden Report

common_name: Blue Paradise Garden Phlox (Fragrant Lavender-Blue Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing at least 18 inches apart for air circulation.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade with good air circulation. Blue Paradise bears large, strongly fragrant flower clusters in a cool lavender-blue that appears deeper blue-violet in the cooler light of morning and evening, one of the closest approaches to true blue in the garden phlox palette, each flower centered with a small magenta-red eye. It blooms over a long season from midsummer into fall and is a strong draw for butterflies, hummingbirds, and evening pollinators drawn by its fragrance. Divide congested clumps every 3–4 years in early spring to maintain vigor and airflow, which helps manage the powdery mildew that affects garden phlox in humid climates.
sources: Mt. Cuba Center — Phlox Trial Garden Report

common_name: Laura Garden Phlox (Purple-Violet with White Eye)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, spacing at least 18 inches apart for air circulation.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade with good air circulation. Laura produces bold, rich purple-violet flowers each marked with a crisp white-and-red central eye, a striking bicolor effect held in large, dense clusters from midsummer into fall on sturdy, upright stems. It ranks among the better mildew-resistant garden phlox cultivars available, holding clean foliage further into the season than many older selections in humid climates, and its saturated color and strong contrast eye make it a standout in a mixed perennial border. Divide congested clumps every 3–4 years in early spring to maintain vigor and airflow, and deadhead spent flowers to prolong bloom and limit self-seeding.
sources: Mt. Cuba Center — Phlox Trial Garden Report

common_name: Balmy Purple Beebalm (Compact Mildew-Resistant Bee Balm)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun, allowing good air circulation.

directions: Plant in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun, allowing good air circulation between plants to reduce powdery mildew. Balmy Purple is part of a compact bee balm series bred for a dense, tidy, mildew-resistant habit far smaller than traditional bee balm, staying under 18 inches while still producing the same tubular purple flower heads that hummingbirds, bees, and butterflies rely on through summer. Its small scale fits border edges and mixed containers where full-size bee balm would be too large, while its improved disease resistance keeps foliage cleaner through humid summers than many older Monarda didyma cultivars. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring to maintain vigor and airflow.
sources: Mt. Cuba Center — Monarda Trial Garden Report

common_name: Carolina Moonlight Baptisia (Yellow-Flowered Hybrid False Indigo)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; baptisia develops a deep taproot and resents being moved once established, so choose its planting site carefully.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun, choosing a permanent site since the deep taproot resents transplanting once established. Carolina Moonlight is one of the earliest and still most popular hybrid baptisia cultivars, producing tall spikes of soft, clear yellow flowers in late spring above blue-green foliage, followed by ornamental dark seed pods that persist into fall and rattle attractively in the wind. Like all baptisias it is exceptionally long-lived, drought-tolerant, and essentially pest-free once established, functioning almost like a flowering shrub in the perennial border despite dying back to the ground each winter. It needs no division and improves in floral display for many years, so give it its full mature spread from the start.

common_name: Solar Flare Baptisia (Yellow-to-Orange-Red Aging False Indigo)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; part of the compact Decadence breeding series, choose its planting site carefully since baptisia resents transplanting once established.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun, choosing a permanent site since the deep taproot resents transplanting once established. Solar Flare produces flower spikes that open golden yellow and shift dramatically to burnt orange and red-orange as they age, so a single spike often shows several colors at once, a striking effect distinct from the solid-color flowers of most baptisia cultivars. Its more compact, Decadence-series habit fits modern garden borders better than the tall, wide-spreading straight species while retaining baptisia's legendary toughness and longevity, and the flowers are followed by ornamental dark seed pods that persist into fall. Established plants are extremely drought-tolerant and essentially pest-free, needing no division and improving for many years.

common_name: Blue Ice Amsonia (Compact Early-Blooming Blue Star)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average to moist soil in full sun to partial shade.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to moist soil in full sun to partial shade. Blue Ice is a compact amsonia hybrid, staying under 15 inches tall while producing especially dense clusters of periwinkle-blue, star-shaped flowers in mid-spring — a deeper, more saturated blue and a longer bloom period than many taller amsonia species. Its small, tidy, mounding habit fits border edges and rock gardens where full-size Amsonia tabernaemontana or A. hubrichtii would be too large, and like other amsonias it is deer-resistant, drought-tolerant once established, and essentially pest-free. No staking or division is needed; the foliage remains an attractive fine texture through summer with good fall color in cooler climates.

common_name: String Theory Amsonia (Dwarf Fine-Textured Threadleaf Blue Star)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average to moist soil in full sun.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to moist soil in full sun. String Theory is a dwarf selection of threadleaf blue star, staying under 18 inches — roughly half the height of the species — while keeping the same finely textured, needle-like foliage and pale blue, star-shaped spring flowers, then putting on the same spectacular golden-yellow fall foliage display the species is prized for. Its smaller scale fits border edges and smaller gardens where full-size Amsonia hubrichtii, which can reach 3 feet, would eventually crowd the space. It is deer-resistant, drought-tolerant once established, and essentially pest-free, needing no staking or routine division.

common_name: Summer Beauty Ornamental Onion (Long-Blooming Pink-Purple Allium)

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring (or fall in mild climates) in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Summer Beauty tolerates more shade and heavier soil than many ornamental onions. It forms a tidy, glossy, deer- and rabbit-resistant clump of strap-like foliage topped from midsummer into early fall by rounded, rosy-purple globe flowers that draw heavy bee and butterfly traffic for weeks — one of the longest bloom periods of any ornamental allium. It performs reliably in the humid Gulf South as long as drainage is adequate, and its glossy foliage resists the rust that can disfigure some ornamental onions in humid climates. Divide congested clumps only when they become crowded after several years; it pairs well with coneflowers, black-eyed Susans, and ornamental grasses in a late-summer pollinator border.
sources: Mt. Cuba Center — Allium Trial Garden Report
